body_html:
The Spanish mistakes learners make are remarkably predictable. After ten years of translating between English and Spanish, I see the same ones again and again in learners’ messages, emails and essays. They come from English habits carried into Spanish: assuming every noun is neutral, translating prepositions one by one, using “to be” for everything. This guide groups them into families, gives you the quick fix for each, and links to a full guide with examples and a quiz.

Key takeaways
  • Most mistakes come from English structures transferred directly into Spanish.
  • They fall into a few families: grammar, words, meaning and writing.
  • Fix one family at a time, using real sentences rather than rules alone.
  • Mistakes are normal; native speakers care far more that you try.
{{toc}}

Why Spanish mistakes are so predictable

Your first language is a template. When Spanish works like English, you speed ahead; when it doesn’t, your brain falls back on the English pattern. That is why learners from different first languages make different mistakes. For learners who speak English, the trouble spots are features English lacks (grammatical gender, the personal a, two verbs for “to be”) and features English does differently (word order, prepositions, the “backwards” structure of gustar). Knowing this is reassuring: your mistakes aren’t random, so they can be fixed systematically.

Grammar and structure mistakes

Noun gender

English nouns are neutral; Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine. The traps are the exceptions: el problema, el día, el mapa, la mano, la foto, and el agua, which is feminine. Fix: always learn nouns with their article. Full guide: {{link:spanish-gender-mistakes|Spanish gender mistakes}}.

Word order

Adjectives usually follow the noun (un carro rojo), object pronouns go before the conjugated verb (Lo veo), and le lo becomes se lo. Full guide: {{link:spanish-word-order|Spanish word order}}.

Prepositions

“Depend on” is depender de, “think about” is pensar en, “look for” is just buscar, and specific people as objects need the personal a: Veo a María. Full guide: {{link:spanish-preposition-mistakes|Spanish preposition mistakes}}.

Gustar

It means “to be pleasing to”, so the thing liked is the subject: Me gustan los perros, never Yo gusto los perros. Full guide: {{link:how-to-use-gustar|how to use gustar}}.

Ser and estar

Two verbs for “to be”, and the meaning can change: Soy aburrido (I’m boring) vs Estoy aburrido (I’m bored). Full guide: {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}.

Also coming in this group: {{link:spanish-article-mistakes|article mistakes}}, {{link:subject-pronouns-in-spanish|overusing subject pronouns}}, {{link:double-negatives-in-spanish|double negatives}} and {{link:spanish-plural-mistakes|plurals}}.

{{image:2}}

Word choice mistakes

Many Spanish mistakes come from one English word splitting into two Spanish words: “ask” (pedir, preguntar), “bring” and “take” (traer, llevar), “play” (jugar, tocar), “but” (pero, sino). I’ve collected all of them, each with a quiz, in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

Then there are false friends, words that look English but aren’t: realizar (to carry out), asistir (to attend), librería (bookshop). See {{link:spanish-false-friends|Spanish false friends}}.

Meaning and manners mistakes

Translating word for word

Spanish says tengo hambre (I have hunger), tengo 30 años and tiene sentido. Idioms almost never transfer: “a piece of cake” is pan comido. Full guide: {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes in Spanish}}.

Embarrassing slips

Embarazada means pregnant, excitado and estoy caliente have sexual meanings, and coger is vulgar in much of Latin America. Full guide: {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}}.

Politeness

Choosing between tú and usted, softening requests and greeting people properly all matter. Start with {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}; a dedicated {{link:spanish-politeness-mistakes|politeness mistakes}} guide is planned.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Writing mistakes

Accent marks are not decoration: si is “if”, sí is “yes”, and año without its ñ becomes a very different word. Full guide: {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}. Planned next: {{link:spanish-punctuation-rules|punctuation with ¿ and ¡}} and {{link:spanish-capitalization-rules|capitalisation}} (days, months and languages are lower case in Spanish).

How to fix your Spanish mistakes for good

1. Work on one family at a time

Spend a week on gender, then a week on prepositions. Trying to fix everything at once fixes nothing.

2. Notice, then collect

When you see the correct form in real Spanish, save the whole sentence. Over time, the correct version simply sounds right. I describe this in {{link:sentence-mining-spanish|sentence mining}}.

3. Read lots of natural Spanish

Mistakes fade fastest through exposure. Reading bilingual books lets you compare English and Spanish structures side by side, which is exactly where these mistakes live; see {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}} and {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input}}.

4. Ask for corrections

Tell Spanish-speaking friends: Corrígeme si me equivoco, por favor (Please correct me if I make a mistake). Most will be happy to help. The Centro Virtual Cervantes is also a reliable free resource for checking grammar.

Final thoughts

The mistakes Spanish learners make are a map of where the two languages differ. Every mistake on this page is one I have made, corrected and eventually forgotten I ever made. Pick one family, read its guide, take the quiz, and come back for the next. And remember: speaking with mistakes is always better than staying silent.

faq.q: What are the most common Spanish mistakes?
faq.a: Noun gender (la problema), gustar structure (yo gusto), ser vs estar, prepositions (depender en), literal translation (estoy hambre), adjective order and missing accent marks.

faq.q: Why do learners make the same mistakes in Spanish?
faq.a: Because they transfer English structures into Spanish, especially where Spanish has features English lacks, such as grammatical gender, the personal a and two verbs for “to be”.

faq.q: How can I stop making mistakes in Spanish?
faq.a: Focus on one mistake family at a time, collect correct example sentences, read lots of natural Spanish and ask native speakers to correct you.
